newsitem.title: GERMANY: Two Turks surrender as Maltese plane hijack ends.
newsitem.headline: Two Turks surrender as Maltese plane hijack ends.

text.p: The hijack of an Air Malta airliner bound for Istanbul with 81 people on board ended peacefully on Monday when two Turks surrendered at Cologne airport, releasing their hostages unharmed, police said.

One of the hijackers with what turned out to be fake explosives strapped to his chest had demanded the release of Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca, who is serving a life sentence in Italy for trying to assassinate the Pope in 1981.

German police quickly established contact with one of the men through a Turkish-speaking interpreter and persuaded him to hand over what appeared to be the fuse of the fake explosive device to the pilot about three hours after landing.
The men left the plane with their arms above their heads accompanied by plain clothes police officers.
"We are thankful the hijack ended without bloodshed," Cologne police chief Juergen Roters told a news conference.
The hijackers gave themselves up after about two hours of negotiations, the police officer in charge of the operation, Winrich Granitzka, said.
"The hijackers made no political demands, they just wanted to attract sympathy for the...assassin (Agca) in a television interview," Roters said.

Granitzka said about 30 minutes into the flight one of the man went into the cockpit and showed the pilot what looked like sticks of dynamite strapped to his chest. He then ordered the pilot to divert to plane to Germany.
The airliner landed at the busy Cologne-Bonn airport 15 km (10 km) south of the city of Cologne at 0247 GMT and stood at a freight section there.
Granitzka said the man eventually handed over a black piece of plastic said to be the fuse to the pilot and the two men surrendered. "The device turned out to be a fake," he said.
Police named the two men as Nosret A., aged 24, and Ismail B., aged 25. Police said Nosret had close links with Germany and prosecutors said he was already wanted here on unspecified charges.

Prosecutors said the two men would be brought before a judge on Tuesday to be formally arrested on charges of a dangerous attack on air traffic. If convicted they could face between five and 15 years in jail.
Police earlier said 90 people were on the flight, including five crew and the two hijackers.

They later revised this figure to 81 and said the 74 passengers comprised 17 Turks, 32 Libyans, 22 Maltese, one Russian, one Tunisian and one German. Some were to fly to Istanbul later on Monday and the rest were to leave on Tuesday.

The hijackers had let five of the passengers leave the plane shortly after landing. One of them was a woman with heart problems, who was treated on the spot. Two others were taken to hospital suffering shock.
During negotiations, the hijackers requested an interview with a television crew in the presence of a human rights group, but before this could take place they gave themselves up.
The hijacking was the first involving an Air Malta aircraft and the first of a flight originating in Malta.
Maltese Prime Minister Afred Sant announced an inquiry into security for the flight and Malta sent a magistrate to Germany to join investigations.
